subtopics.title: Ethanol and E85 Basics
subtopics.summary: Ethanol is a highly purified alcohol that is blended with petrol to make transport fuel. E85 is a blend of 85% ethanol and 15% petrol, and it can be used only in Flex-Fuel Vehicles. The Ethanol Blending Programme is overseen by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.
facts: Ethanol is highly purified alcohol with approximately 99.9% purity.
Major feedstocks for ethanol are sugarcane, maize, wheat and other sugar- and starch-rich crops.
Ethanol blending means mixing ethanol with petrol to create fuel for internal combustion engines.
E85 is a fuel blend of 85% ethanol and 15% petrol (gasoline).
E85 can be used only in Flex-Fuel Vehicles built to run on varying ethanol-petrol blends.
The Ethanol Blending Programme was piloted in 2003 and later expanded under the National Policy on Biofuels (2018).
The Ethanol Blending Programme targeted 20% ethanol blending (E20) by 2030, achieved in 2025.
Nodal ministry for the Ethanol Blending Programme is the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.
Ethanol and biodiesel are the most common biofuels.

subtopics.title: Benefits of Ethanol Blending
subtopics.summary: Ethanol blending is promoted for energy security, environmental gains and farm incomes. It cuts crude oil imports and gives a buffer against price shocks. It also turns agro-waste into fuel and encourages maize over sugarcane.
facts: Import reduction: ethanol cuts India's dependence on crude oil imports.
Blending buffer: ethanol stockpiles give flexibility for price stabilisation against crude oil shocks.
Lifecycle emissions: 2G ethanol reduces GHG emissions by over 50% compared to petrol.
Agro-waste utilisation: stubble, dung and biomass are converted into fuel, supporting a circular economy.
Farmer income: since 2014, farmers have earned about 21 lakh crore through ethanol procurement transfers.
Crop diversification: promotes maize cultivation and reduces over-dependence on sugarcane.
Objectives include reducing crude oil imports and providing assured markets for farmers.

subtopics.title: Concerns with Ethanol Blending
subtopics.summary: A survey finds that many petrol vehicle owners report reduced mileage and higher maintenance costs. Water-intensive sugarcane and land degradation are listed as environmental concerns. Diverting rice and corn for ethanol raises food-versus-fuel questions.
facts: A survey finds 67% of petrol vehicle owners report reduced mileage and higher maintenance costs.
Sugarcane has a high water requirement of 60-70 tonnes per tonne.
Water-intensive sugarcane drives groundwater depletion.
Unsustainable farming causes degradation of nearly 30% of India's land.
Diverting rice and corn for ethanol production raises food-versus-fuel concerns.
Imports and food security concerns are listed as a further issue.

subtopics.title: Biofuel Generations
subtopics.summary: Biofuels are grouped into generations by their feedstock and their carbon impact. First-generation fuels use edible items, while second-generation fuels use leftovers of food crops. Third- and fourth-generation fuels use microorganisms and genetically engineered crops.
facts: 1st generation biofuel is made from edible items such as sugar, corn and starch, and has high carbon content.
2nd generation biofuel is made from leftovers of food crops such as rice husk and wood chips.
2nd generation biofuel has lower greenhouse gas content than 1st generation biofuel.
3rd generation biofuel is produced using microorganisms such as algae and is carbon neutral.
4th generation biofuel is made from genetically engineered crops and is carbon negative.
The National Policy on Biofuels includes production of 2G ethanol as a key element.
A 2G ethanol project is located at Panipat, Haryana.

subtopics.title: Policies, Schemes and Alliances
subtopics.summary: The National Policy on Biofuels aims to reduce import dependence through blending. Schemes such as PM JI-VAN Yojana and GOBAR-DHAN support 2G ethanol and waste-to-energy conversion. India also launched the Global Biofuels Alliance with partner countries in 2023.
facts: National Policy on Biofuels (2018) aims to reduce import dependence by blending bioethanol, biodiesel and Bio-CNG.
PM JI-VAN Yojana (2019) gives financial assistance for developing 2G ethanol from surplus biomass and agricultural waste.
GOBAR-DHAN Scheme (2018) converts cattle dung and solid waste into compost, biogas and bio-CNG.
GOBAR-DHAN was launched under the Swachh Bharat Mission (Gramin).
Repurpose Used Cooking Oil (RUCO) was launched by FSSAI to convert used cooking oil into biodiesel.
BioE3 Policy aims to set up Bio-Foundries that produce biotechnology-developed feedstock and catalysts.
The Cabinet approved a Hydrogen Mission on 04 January 2023 with an outlay of Rs. 19,744 crore.
The Global Biofuels Alliance was launched in 2023 by India on the sidelines of the G20 Summit in New Delhi.
The Global Biofuels Alliance aims to facilitate global biofuel trade and provide technical support for national programmes.

quizzes.passage: Ethanol blending refers to mixing ethanol with petrol to create a fuel that is suitable for internal combustion engines. Ethanol is a highly purified alcohol, and the booklet notes that it can be produced from several major feedstocks, all of them crops that are rich in sugar or starch. The blending programme began as a pilot and has grown in scale over time. The benefits of the programme are discussed under three broad heads. The first head covers energy and economic gains, the second covers environmental gains, and the third covers agricultural and social gains. The booklet lists several points under each head, and each point is a short statement rather than a detailed analysis. The energy and economic head concerns the country's energy position and its economy. The environmental head concerns emissions linked to fuels. The agricultural and social head concerns farmers' income and the choice of crops that they grow. The booklet presents these benefits as the main reasons for promoting ethanol blending. It also records concerns about the programme, which are covered in a separate section of the same chapter. The chapter is part of a wider current affairs discussion on environment and disaster management, and it places the programme within that subject. The subject covers several other topics, but this passage deals only with ethanol blending.

quizzes.passage: Although the booklet describes ethanol blending as a policy with clear aims, it also records a number of concerns about the programme. These concerns fall into two broad groups. The first group concerns the experience of people who drive petrol vehicles, and the second concerns the effects of ethanol production on farming and natural resources. A survey is cited to show how petrol vehicle owners have been affected in everyday use. The owners described changes in how far their vehicles travel on a tank and in what they spend on upkeep. The booklet reports these changes as a concern for vehicle owners and presents the survey as its source. On the environmental side, the booklet points to the crops used for ethanol and to the way land is farmed. It notes that some crops need a large amount of water, and it refers to land that has lost its quality over time. The booklet presents these points as concerns linked to the programme. A further set of concerns relates to the use of some grains for fuel. The booklet lists this alongside the other points. The booklet presents these concerns as a counterpoint to the benefits of the programme, which are discussed separately in the same chapter.

quizzes.passage: Biofuels are fuels made from biomass, and the booklet arranges them into groups called generations. The grouping depends on two things: the feedstock from which a fuel is made, and the amount of carbon that the fuel adds to the air. Because each group is defined by these features, the generations give a simple way to compare one biofuel with another. The booklet describes the groups one after another, beginning with the earliest and moving to newer groups that draw on different inputs and processes. The groups differ in their feedstock and in the carbon impact they are said to have, and the booklet gives a separate account of each one. Biofuel policy is discussed in the same part of the booklet. The National Policy on Biofuels is the framework that the booklet cites, and it aims to reduce import dependence through fuel blending and related production. The accounts are brief, and each one names the feature that separates that group from the others. The booklet uses the terms carbon neutral and carbon negative for two of the groups. Carbon neutral is explained as a case where the carbon emitted equals the carbon sequestrated, and the booklet presents this as a feature of one group.
